idiom_name: using / await using with Symbol.dispose (explicit resource management)
implementation_notes: JavaScript's realization of the pattern is explicit resource management: an object that owns a resource exposes [Symbol.dispose]() (or [Symbol.asyncDispose]() for awaited teardown) and a using declaration disposes it synchronously when its block, function or module body exits - including early return and thrown errors - with multiple bindings disposed in reverse declaration order and errors aggregated into a SuppressedError. Before this shipped, the same contract was hand-written as try/finally around a dispose() call, which is also what transpilers emit; DisposableStack/AsyncDisposableStack exist for stacks of resources and move semantics. Release must be idempotent because the same object can be aliased, and the disposer only releases what the object owns. The scoping caveat is real: a using binding's value can escape the scope that disposes it, and the language does not prevent that.
pitfalls: using disposes at scope exit, but the value can outlive the scope (closures, exports, returns) - re-wrap it with a using at the consumer, or hand-manage it, if the lifetime is longer.
An error thrown by a disposer is aggregated with the body error into a SuppressedError, so a catch for the body error alone will not match.

using is not allowed at the top level of a script or of a switch body (blocks, function bodies, module top level only), and a non-null value whose [Symbol.dispose] is not callable throws a TypeError at the declaration.
